Chapter 1 · 自然地理 / Natural Geography (241 words)

01atmosphere/ˈætməsfɪə(r)/ BrE · /ˈætməsfɪr/ NAmEnoun · B1
Definition
1. (the atmosphere) the mixture of gases that surrounds the earth · 2. a mixture of gases that surrounds another planet or a star · 3. the air in a room or in a small space · 4. the feeling or mood that you have in a particular place or situation.
  • Wind power doesn't release carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo quite different meanings live inside one short word. The earth has an atmosphere (no article in BrE writing, the atmosphere as a singular noun); a room has an atmosphere (countable, can be smoky/stuffy). Don't write “pollution of atmospheres” — the natural one is uncountable.
📖 Oxford: atmosphere
02hydrosphere/ˈhaɪdrəsfɪə(r)/noun
Definition
All the water on the earth's surface, including oceans, seas, rivers, lakes and the water vapour in the air; the water component of the earth.
  • About 71% of the hydrosphere is contained in the oceans.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallDon't pronounce the y as in “why” — it is /haɪ/ as in “high”, and the stress is on HY-dro-sphere. Also: no plural. The earth has one hydrosphere.
📖 Oxford: hydrosphere
03lithosphere/ˈlɪθəsfɪə(r)/noun
Definition
The rigid outer part of the earth, including the crust and the upper part of the mantle; broken into the tectonic plates that carry the continents.
  • The lithosphere is divided into about fifteen major tectonic plates.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress is on LITH-o-sphere, and the th is the soft sound as in “thin”, not “the”. Don't write lithosphere with an s after the t (liths-… is a common misspelling).
📖 Oxford: lithosphere
04oxygen/ˈɒksɪdʒən/ BrE · /ˈɑːksɪdʒən/ NAmEnoun
Definition
A colourless, odourless chemical element (symbol O) that exists as a gas in the atmosphere and is essential for respiration in most living things.
  • Oxygen makes up roughly 21% of the earth's atmosphere.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallBrE /ɒksɪdʒən/ vs NAmE /ɑːksɪdʒən/ — the first vowel is a different vowel. And oxygen is uncountable in nearly every natural use: “a breath of fresh oxygen” sounds wrong. Say “fresh air” or “more oxygen”.
📖 Oxford: oxygen
05oxide/ˈɒksaɪd/ BrE · /ˈɑːksaɪd/ NAmEnoun
Definition
A compound formed when oxygen combines with another chemical element.
  • Iron oxide is the chemical name for rust.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo common traps: (1) Say /ˈɒksaɪd/ “ox-ide”, not /ɒkˈsaɪd/. The stress is on the first syllable. (2) Oxide names in chemistry: “carbon oxide” is rare; the everyday word is carbon monoxide (CO) or carbon dioxide (CO₂). Don't mix them up in Writing Task 1.
📖 Oxford: oxide
06carbon dioxide/ˌkɑːbən daɪˈɒksaɪd/ BrE · /ˌkɑːrbən daɪˈɑːksaɪd/ NAmEnoun
Definition
A colourless, odourless gas (chemical formula CO₂) produced by burning carbon-containing material, by breathing, and by natural processes; the main greenhouse gas from human activity.
  • Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide into the atmosphere.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallWriting “CO2” is fine in informal notes, but in an essay write CO₂ (subscript) or, simpler, just spell out carbon dioxide. And remember it has two syllables in di-oxide: /daɪˈɒk/, not /diˈɒk/.
📖 Oxford: carbon dioxide
07hydrogen/ˈhaɪdrədʒən/noun
Definition
A colourless, odourless, very light gas (symbol H) that combines with oxygen to form water; the most common element in the universe.
  • Hydrogen is the simplest and most abundant element in the universe.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallBrE drops the h in connected speech: /ˈhaɪ-drə-dʒən/ → sounds almost like “high-drij'n”. Don't insert an extra dr and say “hyd-ro-gen” (it is hy-dro-gen: /haɪ-drə-/).
📖 Oxford: hydrogen
08core/kɔː(r)/noun · adj.
Definition
1. the hard central part of a fruit, especially an apple. 2. the central part of the earth, or of any object. 3. the most important or basic part of something.
  • The earth's core is divided into a liquid outer core and a solid inner core.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallDon't say “corse” or “kor” — the vowel is the long /ɔː/ in “more / call / law”. And be careful with spelling: it is core, not core as in “corps” (which is a different word meaning a military unit).
📖 Oxford: core
09crust/krʌst/noun
Definition
1. the hard outer layer or surface of bread, a pie, etc. 2. a layer of something hard, especially one that forms on top of a softer or liquid thing. 3. (geology) the outer layer of the earth.
  • The earth's crust is broken into tectonic plates.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe plural is crusts (with -s, not “crusties” or “crusts” as in “rusts”). And don't confuse crust (the hard outer layer) with crustacean (a sea animal with a shell) — they share a root but mean different things.
📖 Oxford: crust
10mantle/ˈmæntl/noun · verb
Definition
1. (geology) the part of the earth between the crust and the core. 2. a loose, sleeveless cloak worn over other clothes. 3. a covering layer of something. 4. (figurative) a role or responsibility taken on by someone.
  • The upper mantle is solid rock; the lower mantle flows very slowly.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallSpelling trap: mantle (the layer) and mantel (the fireplace shelf) are spelled differently in BrE. Also: mantle is pronounced /ˈmæntl/ — the final e is silent, not “mantle-ee”.
📖 Oxford: mantle
11longitude/ˈlɒŋɡɪtjuːd/ BrE · /ˈlɑːŋɡɪtuːd/ NAmE · /ˈlɒndʒɪtjuːd/ BrE alt.noun
Definition
The distance of a place east or west of a line that runs from the North Pole to the South Pole through Greenwich, London, measured in degrees.
  • Sydney is at longitude 151° east, latitude 34° south.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallDon't pronounce the t in long-i-tude like a t; the t becomes /tʃ/ in BrE (long-i-chude) and stays /t/ in NAmE (long-i-tood). The stress is on LONG.
📖 Oxford: longitude
12latitude/ˈlætɪtjuːd/ BrE · /ˈlætɪtuːd/ NAmEnoun
Definition
1. the distance of a place north or south of the equator, measured in degrees. 2. (figurative) freedom to choose what to do or say.
  • The region lies at a latitude of about 50° north.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallMany learners say “longtitude / longtitude” by mixing up longitude and latitude. A safer pair to drill: long → north–south (pole-to-pole); lat → east–west (like rungs on a ladder).
📖 Oxford: latitude
13altitude/ˈæltɪtjuːd/ BrE · /ˈæltɪtuːd/ NAmEnoun
Definition
1. the height above sea level. 2. (usually plural) a place that is high above sea level.
  • We are flying at an altitude of 6 000 metres.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallAltitude ≠ attitude. They differ by one letter but mean very different things: altitude = height; attitude = a way of thinking. Don't write “a positive altitude to life” — that's attitude. BrE /ˈæltɪtjuːd/ (with the extra y) vs NAmE /ˈæltɪtuːd/.
📖 Oxford: altitude
14horizon/həˈraɪzn/noun
Definition
1. the line at which the earth's surface and the sky appear to meet. 2. (usually plural, figurative) the limit of a person's knowledge, experience or interest.
  • The sun sank below the horizon.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress is on the second syllable: /hə-RAI-zn/. Don't say “HOR-i-zon”. And the noun is usually singular in the literal sense (“the horizon”) but plural in the figurative sense (“broaden your horizons”).
📖 Oxford: horizon
15disaster/dɪˈzɑːstə(r)/ BrE · /dɪˈzæstər/ NAmEnoun
Definition
1. an unexpected event, such as a flood, storm or accident, that causes great damage or loss of life. 2. (informal) a complete failure; a very bad person or thing.
  • Earthquakes, floods and typhoons are all natural disasters.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallBrE and NAmE pronunciation differ on the second vowel: BrE /dɪˈzɑːstə/ (long “ah” as in “bath”); NAmE /dɪˈzæstər/ (“za” as in “fast”). Pick one and stick to it in the exam — mixing them inside one answer is jarring.
📖 Oxford: disaster
16mishap/ˈmɪshæp/noun
Definition
A small accident or piece of bad luck that is not very serious.
  • We arrived home without mishap.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress is on MIS-hap (the first syllable), not “mi-SHAP”. And: mishap is much more polite / humorous than accident in writing. A sentence like “the meeting passed without mishap” is a standard, slightly old-fashioned formal English.
📖 Oxford: mishap
17catastrophic/ˌkætəˈstrɒfɪk/ BrE · /ˌkætəˈstrɑːfɪk/ NAmEadjective
Definition
1. (of a natural event) causing many people to suffer. 2. causing a lot of problems for people.
  • The region was hit by a catastrophic earthquake.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress pattern: cat-a-STRO-phic — the main stress is on STRO, not on “cata-”. The ph in the middle is /f/, not /p/ (it's from Greek -phikos). A very common pronunciation mistake: saying “cat-as-TRO-fik” with the last syllable wrong.
📖 Oxford: catastrophic
18calamity/kəˈlæməti/noun
Definition
An event that causes great damage, suffering or loss; a disaster, especially one that affects many people.
  • The flood was the worst natural calamity in the country's history.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress: ca-LAM-i-ty (the second syllable is loudest). The plural is calamities /kəˈlæmətiz/. Don't write “calamy” or “calamitys”.
📖 Oxford: calamity
19endanger/ɪnˈdeɪndʒə(r)/verb
Definition
To put somebody or something in a situation in which they could be harmed, lost or destroyed.
  • The chemical spill endangered the local water supply.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe prefix is en- (as in enrich, encourage), not in- (as in inside). Don't write “indanger”. And endangered is what you want when you talk about species — not “dangerous species”, which means species that are themselves a threat.
📖 Oxford: endanger
20jeopardise/ˈdʒepədaɪz/verb
Definition
To put something important such as a plan, a job or a relationship at risk of being harmed or lost.
  • A single mistake could jeopardise her career.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallSpelling: British jeopardise / American jeopardize. The OALD main headword is the US spelling jeopardize. For your exam, use one spelling consistently. And jeopardise is a stronger, more literary verb than endanger — reserve it for careers, reputations and big plans, not for spilled coffee.
📖 Oxford: jeopardise
21destructive/dɪˈstrʌktɪv/adjective
Definition
Causing damage or harm; wanting or tending to destroy things.
  • The hurricane was one of the most destructive in decades.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress: de-STRUC-tive (the second syllable is the loudest). The ct cluster in destructive is hard to say for many learners — practise “de-STRUCK-tiv” slowly first.
📖 Oxford: destructive
22El Niño/el ˈniːnjoʊ/ NAmE · /el ˈniːnjəʊ/ BrEnoun
Definition
A climate pattern in which the surface water of the eastern Pacific Ocean becomes unusually warm, affecting weather in many parts of the world; the opposite phase is called La Niña.
  • El Niño events occur every two to seven years.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallIt is two words, capital E capital N, with a tilde over the n in formal writing: El Niño. Pronounce it /el NEE-nyoh/. The plural in normal English is El Niños; in Spanish it is El Niños too (Spanish plurals keep the article in this phrase).
📖 Oxford: El Niño
23greenhouse/ˈɡriːnhaʊs/noun · adj.
Definition
1. (noun) a building made mainly of glass, used for growing plants that need warmth and protection. 2. (as modifier) of or producing the greenhouse effect: greenhouse gas, greenhouse warming.
  • Tomatoes are grown in greenhouses all year round.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallIt's one word: greenhouse (no hyphen). The plural in “two greenhouses” adds a regular -s, but the compound noun “greenhouse gas” uses singular gas as a category: “a greenhouse gas” is fine; “greenhouse gases” also fine in the plural sense.
📖 Oxford: greenhouse
24phenomenon/fəˈnɒmɪnən/ BrE · /fəˈnɑːmɪnən/ NAmEnoun
Definition
1. a fact or an event in nature or society, especially one that is not fully understood. 2. a person or thing that is very successful or impressive. · Plural (sense 1): phenomena /fəˈnɒmɪnə/; (sense 2, NAmE): phenomenons.
  • Globalisation is a phenomenon of the 21st century.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne of the most-frequently-misused words in English. Phenomena is plural; using it as a singular (“a phenomena”) is the classic giveaway. Memorise the trio: criterion / phenomenon / bacterium all follow the Greek pattern -on → -a.
📖 Oxford: phenomenon
25pebble/ˈpebl/noun
Definition
A small, smooth, round stone, especially one found on a beach or in a river.
  • The beach was covered in smooth pebbles.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe consonant cluster pb- in pebble is a pronunciation trap. The b is silent: /ˈpebl/, not “peb-bl”. The plural is pebbles (two syllables, /ˈpeblz/).
📖 Oxford: pebble
26magnet/ˈmæɡnət/noun
Definition
1. a piece of iron or other material that can attract iron or steel. 2. (figurative) a person, place or thing that attracts many people.
  • The fridge was covered with tourist magnets.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe g in magnet is silent: /ˈmænət/, not “mag-net”. The same applies to magnetic /mæɡˈnetɪk/ — the first g is silent, the second is pronounced.
📖 Oxford: magnet
27ore/ɔː(r)/noun
Definition
Rock or earth from which metal or valuable minerals can be obtained.
  • The region is rich in iron ore.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallDon't confuse ore /ɔː/ with oar /ɔː/ (a paddle) and or /ɔː/ (the conjunction). They are homophones. In writing, context is enough: “ore” always appears in a geology/ mining context.
📖 Oxford: ore
28mineral/ˈmɪnərəl/noun · adj.
Definition
1. (noun) a solid, naturally occurring substance that is not a plant or animal, such as gold, salt or quartz. 2. (BrE, plural, often minerals) = mineral water: “a glass of minerals” (BrE). 3. (adjective) of or relating to minerals: mineral deposits / mineral water.
  • Iron and copper are essential minerals for industry.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallIn BrE, the plural minerals can mean mineral water at a restaurant (“two sparkling minerals, please”). NAmE speakers do not use this short form — say mineral water in full.
📖 Oxford: mineral
29marble/ˈmɑːbl/noun · adj.
Definition
1. a hard, usually white or patterned stone, used for buildings and statues. 2. (usually plural) a small glass ball used in children's games. 3. (adjective) made of marble; figurative: cold or smooth like marble.
  • The Parthenon is built of marble.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo unrelated meanings share one spelling. In the geology sense, marble is uncountable: “a slab of marble”. In the toy sense, the plural is marbles — it is also a name for the game: “Let's play marbles.” The adjective sense is rare and literary.
📖 Oxford: marble
30quartz/kwɔːts/noun
Definition
A hard mineral, often in the form of clear or coloured crystals, used in making watches, clocks and electronic circuits.
  • The watch keeps time using a tiny piece of quartz.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallSpelling: quartz has no e after the z (unlike German Quarz). Pronunciation: /kwɔːts/, ending in the cluster /ts/. The plural is quartz (uncountable) or quartzes in technical writing. Don't write “quarts” — that means a unit of volume.
📖 Oxford: quartz
31granite/ˈɡrænɪt/noun
Definition
A very hard, usually grey rock, used for buildings and monuments.
  • The monument is carved out of solid granite.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress is on GRAN-ite. Don't say “gran-EET” or “GRAN-it-eh” — the ending is just one short syllable /ɪt/. The t is fully pronounced.
📖 Oxford: granite
32breeze/briːz/noun · verb
Definition
1. (noun) a light, gentle wind. 2. (informal, countable) something that is easy to do. 3. (verb) to move quickly and lightly.
  • A cool breeze blew in from the sea.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallDon't confuse the noun breeze /briːz/ (light wind) with the verb to breeze through (to do something easily). They share a root but the figurative verb is informal — do not use it in IELTS Writing.
📖 Oxford: breeze
33gust/ɡʌst/noun · verb
Definition
1. (noun) a sudden, short burst of wind, rain, sound, or an emotion. 2. (verb) (of wind) to blow in gusts.
  • A sudden gust of wind blew the hat off her head.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallPronounce the final consonant: /ɡʌst/, not “gus”. And the figurative use — “a gust of laughter”, “a gust of nostalgia” — is a high-frequency IELTS essay phrase.
📖 Oxford: gust
34gale/ɡeɪl/noun
Definition
1. a very strong wind; on the Beaufort scale, a gale is roughly force 8–10. 2. (figurative) a sudden loud burst of noise, e.g. laughter.
  • The coast was battered by gale-force winds.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallDon't rhyme it with “pale” — it is /ɡeɪl/ like the man's name Gael / gale (rhymes with “fail” in some accents and “bell” in others — but the standard pronunciation is rhymes with “pale”).
📖 Oxford: gale
35hurricane/ˈhʌrɪkən/ BrE · /ˈhɜːrɪkeɪn/ NAmEnoun
Definition
A violent storm with extremely strong winds and heavy rain, especially in the western Atlantic Ocean. (Same phenomenon is called a typhoon in the western Pacific and a cyclone in the Indian Ocean.)
  • New Orleans was devastated by Hurricane Katrina in 2005.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallPronunciation: BrE /ˈhʌrɪkən/ (three syllables, stress on the first), NAmE /ˈhɜːrɪkeɪn/ (two syllables, rhymes with “cane”). Don't use the NAmE pronunciation in a BrE exam or vice versa — pick one and stick to it.
📖 Oxford: hurricane
36tornado/tɔːˈneɪdəʊ/ BrE · /tɔːrˈneɪdoʊ/ NAmEnoun
Definition
A violent storm with very strong winds that spin extremely fast and form a funnel-shaped cloud that touches the ground; common in central US in spring and summer. (Also called twister in informal NAmE.)
  • The tornado flattened the entire town in under a minute.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress: tor-NAY-do. Plural: tornadoes /tɔːˈneɪdəʊz/ (BrE also accepts tornados, but tornadoes is preferred). Don't write “tornadoes” as if it were Italian: “tornadi” is wrong.
📖 Oxford: tornado
37typhoon/taɪˈfuːn/noun
Definition
A violent tropical storm with very strong winds, occurring especially in the western Pacific Ocean. (Same phenomenon as a hurricane in the Atlantic / a cyclone in the Indian Ocean.)
  • The Philippines was hit by Typhoon Haiyan in 2013.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe spelling typhoon is sometimes mixed up with taifun or taifoon (German) or taifun. The English spelling is typhoon, two os, one ph. Stress: ty-FOON.
📖 Oxford: typhoon
38monsoon/ˌmɒnˈsuːn/ BrE · /ˌmɑːnˈsuːn/ NAmEnoun · C1
Definition
1. a period of heavy rain in summer in South Asia; the rain that falls during this period. 2. a wind in South Asia that blows from the south-west in summer, bringing rain, and the north-east in winter.
  • Travelling is much more difficult during the monsoon.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallPronounce the ns as /ns/, not /nz/: /mɒnˈsuːn/, not “mon-zoo-n”. The oo is a long /uː/ as in “moon”. And remember: it's not only rain. Monsoon is also the wind that brings the rain.
📖 Oxford: monsoon
39volcano/vɒlˈkeɪnəʊ/ BrE · /vɑːlˈkeɪnoʊ/ NAmEnoun
Definition
A mountain or hill with a hole at the top through which gases, hot liquid rock (lava) and ash can escape from deep inside the earth.
  • Mount Etna is an active volcano in Sicily.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallPronunciation: /vɒl-KAY-noh/ — stress on the second syllable, not the first. Plural: volcanoes (preferred) or volcanos. Don't write “volcanos” if you can avoid it — the standard plural is -oes.
📖 Oxford: volcano
40erupt/ɪˈrʌpt/verb
Definition
1. (of a volcano) to throw out burning rocks, ash and lava. 2. (of a person or feelings) to become suddenly and violently loud or active. 3. (of violence, fighting, etc.) to start suddenly.
  • The volcano erupted without warning, sending ash 10 km into the air.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe noun is eruption (one p before the -tion: rup → ruption). Don't write “eruption” as “eruption” — wait, the spelling is correct, but people sometimes write “eruption” correctly and then misspell the verb as “eruption” by analogy. The verb is erupt; the noun is eruption.
📖 Oxford: erupt
41magma/ˈmæɡmə/noun
Definition
Hot, liquid rock found below the earth's surface. When it reaches the surface it is called lava.
  • The magma chamber lies a few kilometres below the volcano.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallPronounce it /ˈmæɡmə/ — both syllables get full vowels, the g is hard, the final a is a schwa. Don't say “mag-ma” with a long second vowel, and don't drop the first g.
📖 Oxford: magma
42thermodynamic/ˌθɜːməʊdaɪˈnæmɪk/ BrE · /ˌθɜːrmoʊdaɪˈnæmɪk/ NAmEadjective
Definition
Relating to the branch of physics that deals with the relationship between heat, work, temperature and energy.
  • Engineers applied thermodynamic principles to design a more efficient turbine.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress: ther-mo-dy-NAM-ic (the third syllable is the loudest). The th at the start is the soft /θ/ as in “thin”, not the hard /ð/ as in “the”. Don't say “ther-mo-DIE-namic”.
📖 Oxford: thermodynamic
43smog/smɒɡ/ BrE · /smɑːɡ/ NAmEnoun
Definition
A form of air pollution that is a mixture of smoke and fog, especially in big cities.
  • The city was covered in a thick layer of smog.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe word is one syllable: /smɒɡ/ (BrE rhymes with “fog”). Don't insert an extra vowel and say “smog-ee”. The plural is unusual: smog is uncountable in standard usage.
📖 Oxford: smog
44fume/fjuːm/noun · verb
Definition
1. (noun, usually plural) smoke or gas that has an unpleasant smell, especially from a chemical or car engine. 2. (verb) to be very angry; to give off fumes.
  • The workshop was full of petrol fumes.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallIn BrE, fume rhymes with “flew” (/fjuːm/); in NAmE the /j/ sound can be reduced to /fjuːm/ or even /fuːm/. Don't say “fume” like “boom” — the final m is a real consonant.
📖 Oxford: fume
45mist/mɪst/noun · verb
Definition
1. (noun) a thin cloud of very small drops of water in the air, near the ground. 2. a film of moisture that makes it difficult to see clearly. 3. (verb) to cover or become covered with mist.
  • The hills were hidden by early morning mist.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallShort vowel: /mɪst/ like “missed”, not “moist” (which is a different word with a long vowel). The s and t form a final cluster, so the word is one syllable.
📖 Oxford: mist
46tsunami/tsuːˈnɑːmi/noun · B2
Definition
An extremely large wave in the sea caused, for example, by an earthquake under the sea.
  • A tsunami early-warning system was set up in Hawaii.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallPronounce it /tsuː-NAA-mi/ (stress on the second syllable). The initial ts is a single affricate sound, like in “cats” — don't break it into two syllables “t-su”. The plural is tsunamis /tsuːˈnɑːmiz/.
📖 Oxford: tsunami
47flooding/ˈflʌdɪŋ/noun
Definition
A situation in which an area of land is covered with water, especially when this causes damage; the action of being covered with water.
  • Severe flooding forced thousands to leave their homes.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallFlooding is a noun formed from the verb flood; do not use it as an adjective. Say “flooded areas”, not “flooding areas” (which would mean “areas that are flooding something else” — wrong). Also: inundation is the very formal alternative if you need a Band 9.0 word.
📖 Oxford: flooding
48torrent/ˈtɒrənt/ BrE · /ˈtɔːrənt/ NAmEnoun
Definition
1. a large amount of water moving very quickly and strongly. 2. a sudden large amount of something that comes in a stream.

Chapter 2 · 植物研究 / Plant Research (130 words)

01photosynthesis/ˌfəʊtəʊˈsɪnθəsɪs/noun
Definition
The process by which green plants use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose (sugar) and oxygen.
  • Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the leaves.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallSix syllables — stress is on the third one: pho-to-SYN-the-sis. Many learners stress the first syllable, which makes it sound like a different word. And do not say “photosyntesis” — the th is real (/θ/).
📖 Oxford: photosynthesis
02respire/rɪˈspaɪə(r)/verb
Definition
1. (formal) to breathe. 2. (biology) for a plant or animal to take in oxygen from air or water and release carbon dioxide.
  • Fish respire through their gills.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe verb respire is technical / formal; in everyday English we just say breathe. In IELTS writing about plant biology, “plants respire continuously” is sharper than “plants breathe all the time” — but never use respire for a person unless you are in a medical textbook.
📖 Oxford: respire
03botany/ˈbɒtəni/ BrE · /ˈbɑːtəni/ NAmEnoun
Definition
The scientific study of plants.
  • She has a degree in botany from Cambridge.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress is on the first syllable: BOT-a-ny, not “bo-TA-ny”. And the adjective form is botanical (not “botanic”): “a botanical garden”, “botanical illustrations”.
📖 Oxford: botany
04ecology/iˈkɒlədʒi/ BrE · /iˈkɑːlədʒi/ NAmEnoun
Definition
1. the scientific study of the relationship between living things and their environment. 2. the pattern of relations between a particular group of organisms and their environment.
  • She is a professor of plant ecology.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallPronounce the second syllable like “call”, not like “cold”: /i-KO-lə-dʒi/. And ecology ≠ economy. The o in the second syllable carries a lot of weight — slurring them together is the most common student mistake.
📖 Oxford: ecology
05ecosystem/ˈiːkəʊsɪstəm/ BrE · /ˈiːkoʊsɪstəm/ NAmEnoun
Definition
All the living things in an area and the way they affect each other and the environment.
  • The Amazon ecosystem is one of the most diverse on earth.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress is on EE-co-sys-tem — three stresses almost equally, with the strongest on the first syllable. Don't put full stress on “-sys-”; that makes it sound like a different word. The plural is ecosystems.
📖 Oxford: ecosystem
06eco-friendly/ˌiːkəʊˈfrendli/adjective
Definition
Not harmful to the environment; designed to cause as little harm as possible to the environment.
  • Switch to eco-friendly cleaning products.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallAlways written with a hyphen: eco-friendly. And in formal writing prefer environmentally friendly or just sustainable — “eco-friendly” is a touch informal / marketing-ish.
📖 Oxford: eco-friendly
07vegetation/ˌvedʒəˈteɪʃn/noun
Definition
Plants in general, or the plants that are found in a particular place.
  • The island is covered in dense tropical vegetation.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress is on the third syllable: ve-ge-TA-tion. The noun is always singular and uncountable: “the vegetation of the region” — never “vegetations”. And don't say “vegetations” to mean “kinds of plants”; use plants or flora.
📖 Oxford: vegetation
08herb/hɜːb/ BrE · /ɜːrb/ NAmEnoun
Definition
1. a plant whose leaves, flowers or seeds are used to give flavour to food, or as medicine. 2. (also herb /hɜːb/) a soft, leafy plant without woody stems.
  • Rosemary and thyme are common cooking herbs.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallPronunciation is one of the classic BrE / NAmE splits: BrE /hɜːb/ (silent h); NAmE /ɜːrb/ (the h is pronounced). The r in NAmE is the giveaway. Don't write “erb” in BrE spelling.
📖 Oxford: herb
09perennial/pəˈreniəl/noun · adj.
Definition
1. (noun) a plant that lives for several years (compare annual, biennial). 2. (adjective) lasting for a long time; happening again and again.
  • Roses are popular perennials in temperate gardens.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe noun is perennial (one l, two ns), the adjective is the same form. Stress: pe-REN-ni-al (the second n is silent, like in “happen”). Don't double the second n and say “perrenial”.

10horticulture/ˈhɔːtɪkʌltʃə(r)/noun
Definition
The study and practice of growing plants, flowers and fruit.
  • She studied horticulture before opening her own nursery.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress is on the first syllable: HOR-ti-cul-ture. Don't rhyme it with “culture” on the second-to-last syllable. The ch in the middle is /tʃ/ (as in “church”), not /k/.

11organism/ˈɔːɡənɪzəm/ BrE · /ˈɔːrɡənɪzəm/ NAmEnoun

a change, especially in amount, level or form; a different form of something.

the quality or fact of including many different types of people or things; the range of different types.

Definition
1. to develop gradually, especially from a simple to a more complex form. 2. to develop a plan, idea, etc. in this way.

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress: e-VOLVE (second syllable). The v is pronounced; the final e is silent. Don't write “evlove” or say “EE-volve”.
📖 Oxford: evolve
20fluctuate/ˈflʌktʃueɪt/verb
Definition
To change frequently; to rise and fall irregularly.
  • Prices fluctuate according to demand.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress: FLUC-tu-ate (first syllable). The middle tu is pronounced /tʃu/ (as in “century”). Don't pronounce it /tuː/ with a long u.
📖 Oxford: fluctuate
21cultivate/ˈkʌltɪveɪt/verb
Definition
1. to prepare and use land for growing plants. 2. to develop a skill, an ability, a feeling, etc. 3. to try to develop a friendship or a relationship with somebody.
  • The land has been cultivated for generations.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress: CUL-ti-vate (first syllable). The final -ate is pronounced /eɪt/ (like “late”). Don't write “cultavate” or “cultavete”.

22sow/səʊ/verb
Definition
1. to plant or scatter seeds in or on the ground. 2. (figurative) to introduce or spread feelings or ideas.
  • Farmers sow wheat in autumn.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallDon't confuse sow /səʊ/ (plant seeds) with sew /səʊ/ (stitch with thread) or so /səʊ/ (very). They all sound almost identical in fast speech; context is the only clue. Say /səʊ/ carefully when ambiguity is possible.
📖 Oxford: sow
23harvest/ˈhɑːvɪst/ BrE · /ˈhɑːrvɪst/ NAmEnoun · verb
Definition
1. the time of year when crops are cut and gathered from the fields. 2. the crops cut and gathered. 3. (verb) to cut and gather a crop. 4. (figurative) the result of an action.
  • This year's wheat harvest was the best in a decade.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallPronounce the h clearly: /ˈhɑː-vist/, not “arvest”. And the r in NAmE links to the following vowel — “harv-ist” — but in BrE the r is silent unless followed by a vowel.
📖 Oxford: harvest
24pluck/plʌk/verb
Definition
1. to pull or pick something, especially with the fingers. 2. to remove the feathers from a chicken or other bird. 3. (figurative) to pull somebody out of a dangerous or unpleasant situation.
  • She plucked a daisy from the lawn.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallDon't confuse pluck (pick / pull) with plank (a board) or plunk (to drop heavily, informal). The u in pluck is short /ʌ/ (as in “luck”).
📖 Oxford: pluck
25pick/pɪk/verb · noun
Definition
1. to choose somebody or something from a group. 2. to take flowers, fruit, etc. from the plant or tree by hand. 3. to remove small pieces of something from a surface.
  • You can pick the team you want to be in.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallShort vowel /ɪ/ (as in “pit”). Pick and peak are often confused in spelling — “pick a peak” is wrong; it is pick a peak only if you mean a peak chosen; normally “climb a peak” or “pick a winner”. Don't mix the two.
📖 Oxford: pick
26yield/jiːld/noun · verb
Definition
1. (noun) the total amount of crops, profits, etc. produced. 2. (noun, finance) the income from an investment. 3. (verb) to produce a result, profit, etc. 4. (verb) to give way to pressure or persuasion.

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOld-fashioned spelling: past tense & past participle are both yielded, not “yold” or “yolden” (which don't exist). And the ie in yield is pronounced /iː/ (as in “feel”), not /ɪ/ or /aɪ/.
📖 Oxford: yield
27rear/rɪə(r)/verb · adj.
Definition
1. (verb) to care for young children or animals until they are fully grown. 2. (verb) to breed or grow animals or plants. 3. (adjective, only before noun) at the back of something.
  • She reared five children on her own.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallBrE pronunciation is /rɪə/ (rhymes with “beer”); NAmE is /rɪr/ (rhymes with “rear” written — same as the spelling). Don't confuse rear with rear the noun / adjective (same spelling) — the stress is the same but the grammar differs.

28arable/ˈærəbl/adjective
Definition
(of land) suitable or used for growing crops.
  • Only 8% of the country's land is arable.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress on the first syllable: AR-a-ble. Pronounce the final /bl/ clearly — don't say “arra-bull”. The adjective has no noun form: if you need a noun, say arable land or cropland.
📖 Oxford: arable
29plough/plaʊ/noun · verb
Definition
1. (noun) a large farming implement with blades, used to turn the soil and make it ready for planting. 2. (verb) to turn over the surface of soil using a plough.
  • The farmer was ploughing the field.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallSpelling: plough BrE / plow NAmE. Don't use the American spelling in a BrE exam, or vice versa. Pronounce /plaʊ/ (rhymes with “now”).
📖 Oxford: plough
30spade/speɪd/noun
Definition
A tool with a sharp metal blade and a long handle, used for digging.
  • She dug the hole with a spade.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe idiom call a spade a spade is becoming less common; use it only if you are sure of the audience. A more modern alternative is “let's be straightforward”. Pronounce /speɪd/ (the ea is a long e as in “day”).
📖 Oxford: spade
31rake/reɪk/noun · verb
Definition
1. a garden tool with a long handle and a row of metal prongs at the end. 2. (verb) to gather leaves or smooth soil with a rake.
  • In autumn, we rake up the leaves.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe verb rake is also a slang term meaning to criticize a person or their work severely (often in journalism). Don't confuse with wreck /rek/ (destroy).
📖 Oxford: rake
32stack/stæk/noun · verb
Definition
1. (noun) a pile of things, one on top of another. 2. (verb) to put things into a pile. 3. (informal) a large amount of something.
  • A stack of letters waited on the desk.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallIn British English, the compound haystack has no plural; you say “three haystacks”. The word stacks (plural, informal for “a lot”) is very common in speaking: “I've got stacks to do.”

33heap/hiːp/noun · verb
Definition
1. a large untidy pile of things. 2. (informal) a large amount of something. 3. (informal, especially NAmE) an old, broken car.
  • Her clothes lay in a heap on the floor.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress the ea as a long /iː/ (as in “heap”), not as /ɛ/ (as in “head”). And heaps of in informal BrE = “a lot of”: “Heaps of fun!”
📖 Oxford: heap
34bundle/ˈbʌndl/noun · verb
Definition
1. a number of things tied or wrapped together. 2. a collection of things. 3. (informal) a large amount of money.
  • She carried a bundle of clothes to the recycling bin.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallDon't confuse bundle (a tied bunch) with bundle the verb: “she was bundled into the car” means she was pushed / forced, often roughly. In casual BrE “a bundle” alone = “a lot of money”.

35bunch/bʌntʃ/noun · verb
Definition
1. a number of things of the same type, fastened or growing together. 2. a small group of people. 3. (informal) thanks a bunch (= thank you, often sarcastic).
  • She picked a bunch of wild flowers.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallUse bunch for things naturally clustered — flowers, grapes, bananas, keys. Don't say “a bunch of sugar” or “a bunch of friends” (the second is informal but acceptable; the first is wrong). The ch at the end is /tʃ/ (as in “church”).

36vase/vɑːz/ BrE · /veɪs/ NAmEnoun
Definition
A container, usually tall and made of glass or pottery, used for displaying cut flowers.
  • She put the roses in a blue vase.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallPronunciation: BrE and NAmE differ. In BrE both /vɑːz/ and /veɪz/ are accepted. In NAmE the standard is /veɪs/. Don't rhyme it with “gaze” /geɪz/ unless you are speaking old-fashioned BrE.
📖 Oxford: vase
37sunlight/ˈsʌnlaɪt/noun
Definition
The light from the sun.
  • The plants need several hours of direct sunlight.

Definition
Any plant without leaves, flowers or green colouring, often growing on other plants or on decaying matter, e.g. mushrooms, mould, yeast.

📖 Oxford: fungus
39mould/məʊld/ BrE · /moʊld/ NAmEnoun · verb
Definition
1. a soft green or grey fungus that grows on old food or damp objects. 2. a hollow container used to give shape to a liquid or soft substance. 3. (verb) to shape a soft substance into a particular form.

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe BrE noun is spelled mould (with -ou-); the NAmE spelling is mold. In BrE writing, always use mould. Pronounce /məʊld/ (rhymes with “cold” in BrE, “mold” in NAmE).
📖 Oxford: mould
40pollen/ˈpɒlən/ BrE · /ˈpɑːlən/ NAmEnoun
Definition
Fine powder produced by the male part of a flower, used in fertilising other flowers.
  • Bees carry pollen from flower to flower.

📖 Oxford: pollen
41germinate/ˈdʒɜːmɪneɪt/ BrE · /ˈdʒɜːrmɪneɪt/ NAmEverb
Definition
1. (of a seed) to start growing, producing roots and shoots. 2. (of a plant) to produce roots and shoots.
  • Seeds need warmth and water to germinate.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress is on the first syllable: GER-mi-nate. Don't confuse with terminate (to end) or illuminate (to light up). And the noun form is germination (one m after the r; the e is dropped in the spelling: ger-min-ate).

42seed/siːd/noun · verb
Definition
1. (noun) the small, hard part of a plant, from which a new plant grows. 2. (verb) to plant seeds. 3. (idiom) go to seed — to become weaker or untidy.

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe ee in seed is a long /iː/ (as in “see”), not /e/ (as in “said”). The idiom go to seed is slightly old-fashioned but still very common in BrE — a graceful alternative to “get worse” in Writing.

Definition
To begin to grow or develop rapidly; to flourish.
  • The city's tech sector has burgeoned in the last decade.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThe u in burgeon is pronounced /ɜː/ (as in “bird”), not /ʌ/ (as in “but”). Stress on the first syllable: BUR-geon. Use it mainly in formal writing — “a burgeoning market” is a Band 7+ upgrade over “a fast-growing market”.

Definition
1. (noun) a small, tight part that grows on a plant and from which a flower or leaf develops. 2. (verb) to produce buds.

46blossom/ˈblɒsəm/ BrE · /ˈblɑːsəm/ NAmEnoun · verb
Definition

47bloom/bluːm/noun · verb

Definition

51fruit/fruːt/noun · verb

Definition
Grass that has been cut and dried, used as food for animals.

Definition

Definition

Definition
1. a common wild plant with thin green leaves that covers the ground. 2. (slang) marijuana. 3. (informal) a person who informs on others.
  • The grass was wet with dew.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne syllable. Usually uncountable when referring to lawns. The compound grassland is an ecosystem. The phrase to grass on somebody (BrE informal) means to inform on.
📖 Oxford: grass
81meadow/ˈmedəʊ/noun
Definition
A field of grass, used for making hay.
  • Cows grazed in the meadow.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables: MEAD-ow. The compound water meadow / alpine meadow is common. Don't confuse with meadow and shallow.
📖 Oxford: meadow
82lawn/lɔːn/noun
Definition
An area of ground covered with short grass, usually in a garden or park.
  • She mowed the lawn on Saturday.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne syllable. The compound lawn mower / lawn tennis is common. The phrase lawn party is NAmE. Don't confuse with lawn and loan.
📖 Oxford: lawn
83olive/ˈɒlɪv/noun
Definition
1. a small green or black fruit with a bitter taste, used for food and for oil. 2. (also olive tree) the tree on which this fruit grows. 3. (also olive green) a yellowish-green colour.
  • Olive trees grow well in Mediterranean climates.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables: OL-ive. The compound olive oil / olive branch (= a symbol of peace) is common. Don't confuse with olive and olive.
📖 Oxford: olive
84pine/paɪn/noun
Definition
1. an evergreen tree with needles and cones. 2. (also pinewood) the wood of this tree. Verb: (literary) to feel a deep sadness.
  • Pine trees covered the mountain.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne syllable. The compound pine cone / pine forest is common. The verb to pine for means to miss somebody/something greatly.
📖 Oxford: pine
85vine/vaɪn/noun
Definition
1. a plant that climbs up a wall or along the ground. 2. (also grapevine) a plant that produces grapes.
  • Grapes grew on the vine.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne syllable. The compound vineyard is a place where grapes are grown. The phrase heard it through the grapevine is figurative (informal news).
📖 Oxford: vine
86violet/ˈvaɪələt/noun
Definition
1. a small plant with purple or white flowers that bloom in spring. 2. a bluish-purple colour. Adjective: bluish-purple.
  • Violets bloomed in the garden.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThree syllables: VI-o-let. Stress on the first syllable. The compound shrinking violet (= a very shy person) is figurative. Don't confuse with violet and violent.
📖 Oxford: violet
87tulip/ˈtjuːlɪp/noun
Definition
A plant that grows from a bulb, with large brightly coloured flowers in spring.
  • Tulips bloomed in the Dutch fields.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables: TU-lip. The compound tulip festival is common. The phrase tulip mania refers to a famous 17th-century economic bubble in the Netherlands.
📖 Oxford: tulip
88mint/mɪnt/noun
Definition
1. a herb whose leaves are used for flavouring food. 2. a place where coins are made. Verb: to make a coin. 3. (informal) a large amount of money.
  • She made tea with fresh mint.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne syllable. The compound mint leaf / peppermint is common. The phrase in mint condition means perfect condition. Don't confuse mint (the herb) with mint (the coin place).
📖 Oxford: mint
89reef/riːf/noun
Definition
A long line of rocks or sand near the surface of the sea.
  • Coral reefs are home to many fish.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne syllable. The compound coral reef / barrier reef is common. The plural is reefs. The verb to reef (sailing) means to reduce the area of a sail.
📖 Oxford: reef
90alga/ˈælɡə/noun
Definition
A very simple plant that lives in or near water and has no real leaves, stems or roots.

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables: AL-ga. The plural is algae /ˈælɡiː/ or /ˈældʒiː/. The adjective is algal. The compound algal bloom is a Writing Task 1 topic.
📖 Oxford: alga
91enzyme/ˈenzaɪm/noun

A substance produced by living cells that causes a chemical change without being changed itself.

📖 Oxford: enzyme
92catalyst/ˈkætəlɪst/noun
Definition

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThree syllables: CAT-a-lyst. The verb is to catalyse. The compound catalyst for change is a common Writing Task 2 collocation.
📖 Oxford: catalyst
93release/rɪˈliːs/verb
Definition

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables: re-LEASE. The compound press release / release date is common. Don't confuse with re-lease (lease again).
📖 Oxford: release
94emission/iˈmɪʃn/noun
Definition
1. the act of sending out gas, heat, light, etc. 2. gas, heat, or light that is sent out.

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThree syllables: e-MIS-sion. Stress on the second syllable. The verb is to emit. The compound carbon emissions / greenhouse gas emissions is common.
📖 Oxford: emission
95absorb/əbˈzɔːb/verb

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne syllable. The noun is absorption. The compound absorb nutrients is common. Don't confuse with absorb and adsorb (a chemistry term).

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallFour syllables: cir-cu-LA-tion. Stress on the third syllable. The verb is to circulate. The compound atmospheric circulation is a Writing Task 1 topic.
📖 Oxford: circulation
97exceed/ɪkˈsiːd/verb
Definition
To be greater than a number or amount.

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables: ex-CEED. The noun is excess. The adjective is excessive. The compound exceed the limit is common.
📖 Oxford: exceed

Definition

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThree syllables: NU-tri-ent. Stress on the first syllable. The adjective is nutritious (= full of nutrients). The compound nutrient absorption is a Writing Task 1 topic.
📖 Oxford: nutrient
100energy/ˈenədʒi/noun
Definition

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThree syllables: EN-er-gy. The adjective is energetic. The compound solar energy / renewable energy is common in Writing Task 1.
📖 Oxford: energy
101surroundings/səˈraʊndɪŋz/noun
Definition
Everything that is around a place; the environment.

Definition

Definition

Definition

110ruin/ˈruːɪn/verb

111perish/ˈperɪʃ/verb
Definition

Definition

113infringe/ɪnˈfrɪndʒ/verb

114undermine/ˌʌndəˈmaɪn/verb
Definition

115extinction/ɪkˈstɪŋkʃn/noun

116pattern/ˈpætn/noun

Definition
A thing that is a result or consequence of an action, situation, etc.

118impact/ˈɪmpækt/noun

Definition
Connected with a particular season; happening or needed during a season.

121favourable/ˈfeɪvərəbl/adjective
Definition

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThree syllables: FA-vour-able. BrE: favourable; NAmE: favorable. The noun is favour. The compound favourable conditions is a Writing Task 1 topic.

122productive/prəˈdʌktɪv/adjective
Definition
1. producing or able to produce large amounts of goods or crops. 2. (of land) producing good crops.

123effective/ɪˈfektɪv/adjective
Definition
1. producing the result that is wanted. 2. (of a law, system, etc.) having an effect.

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThree syllables: ef-FEC-tive. The noun is effectiveness. The compound effective measure / highly effective is common in Writing Task 2. Don't confuse with efficient.

124efficient/ɪˈfɪʃnt/adjective
Definition
1. doing something well without wasting time, money, or energy. 2. (of a machine or system) working well.

⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThree syllables: ef-FI-cient. The noun is efficiency. The compound energy-efficient / cost-efficient is common. Don't confuse with effective.

Definition
Great in amount, size, or importance.

126massive/ˈmæsɪv/adjective
Definition
1. extremely large, heavy, or solid. 2. (informal) very successful or popular.

127immense/ɪˈmens/adjective
Definition
Extremely large or great.

As great or as large as possible.

129minimal/ˈmɪnɪməl/adjective
Definition
As small or as little as possible.

Definition
Best; most favourable.

Chapter 3 · 动物保护 / Animal Protection (Wildlife Conservation) (169 words)

01biologist/baɪˈɒlədʒɪst/noun
Definition
1. a scientist who studies biology
★ Collocations: distinguished biologist; prominent biologist; senior biologist
★ Word family: biologistic (adj)
  • Marine biologists study ocean life.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress on the second syllable: bi-OL-o-gist. The adjective is biological; the field is biology.
📖 Oxford: biologist
02zoologist/zuˈɒlədʒɪst/noun
Definition
1. a scientist who studies zoology
★ Word family: zoologistic (adj)
  • Zoologists tag wild animals to track their movements.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress on the second syllable: zo-OL-o-gist. From Greek zoion (animal). The field is zoology.
📖 Oxford: zoologist
03ecologist/iˈkɒlədʒɪst/noun
Definition
1. a scientist who studies ecology
2. a person who is interested in ecology
★ Word family: ecologistic (adj)
  • Ecologists warn about the loss of biodiversity.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress on the second syllable: e-COL-o-gist. The field is ecology.
📖 Oxford: ecologist
04botanist/ˈbɒtənɪst/noun
Definition
1. a scientist who studies botany
★ Word family: botanistic (adj)
  • The botanist discovered a new species of orchid.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThree syllables: BOT-a-nist. Stress on the first syllable. The field is botany.
📖 Oxford: botanist
05mammal/ˈmæml/noun
Definition
1. any animal that gives birth to live young, not eggs, and feeds its young on milk. Cows, humans and whales
★ Collocations: large mammal; small mammal; higher mammal
★ Word family: mammalian (adj); mammalia (n, plural)
  • Whales, bats, and humans are all mammals.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne syllable: MAM-ml. The plural is mammals; don't say “mammalies”.
📖 Oxford: mammal
06primate/ˈpraɪmeɪt/noun
Definition
1. any animal that belongs to the group of mammals
2. an archbishop
★ Collocations: higher primates; non-human primates
★ Word family: primatal (adj); primatology (n)
  • Monkeys and apes are primates.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables: PRY-mate. Don't confuse with archpriest (a senior priest).
📖 Oxford: primate
07vertebrate/ˈvɜːtɪbrət/noun
Definition
1. having a backbone
★ Collocations: higher vertebrates; cold-blooded vertebrates
★ Word family: invertebrate (adj/n, opposite)
  • Fish are vertebrates; insects are not.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallStress on the first syllable: VER-te-brate. The adjective is vertebral.
📖 Oxford: vertebrate
08reptile/ˈreptaɪl/noun
Definition
1. any animal that has cold blood and skin covered in scales
★ Collocations: cold-blooded reptiles; tropical reptiles
★ Word family: reptilian (adj); reptilia (n, plural)
  • Snakes and lizards are common reptiles.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables: REP-tile. Stress on the first syllable. The adjective is reptilian.
📖 Oxford: reptile
09amphibian/æmˈfɪbiən/noun
Definition
1. any animal that can live both on land and in water. Amphibians
★ Collocations: aquatic amphibians; tailed amphibians
★ Word family: amphibious (adj); amphibia (n, plural)
  • Frogs and newts are common amphibians.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallFive syllables: am-PHI-bi-an. Stress on the third syllable. The adjective is amphibious.
📖 Oxford: amphibian
10carnivore/ˈkɑːnɪvɔː(r)/noun
Definition
1. any animal that eats meat
★ Collocations: large carnivores; apex carnivores; social carnivores
★ Word family: carnivorous (adj); carnivory (n)
  • Lions are obligate carnivores.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThree syllables: CAR-ni-vore. Stress on the first syllable. The adjective is carnivorous.
📖 Oxford: carnivore
11herbivore/ˈhɜːbɪvɔː(r)/noun
Definition
1. any animal that eats only plants
★ Collocations: large herbivores; grazing herbivores
★ Word family: herbivorous (adj); herbivory (n)
  • Cows are herbivores.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallThree syllables: HER-bi-vore. Stress on the first syllable. Don't confuse with herbivorous.
📖 Oxford: herbivore
12creature/ˈkriːtʃə(r)/noun
Definition
1. a living thing, real or imaginary, that can move around, such as an animal
2. a person, considered in a particular way
3. a person or thing that depends completely on somebody else and is controlled by them
★ Collocations: living creature; primitive creature; simple creature
★ Word family: creatural (adj, rare)
  • The deep sea is full of strange creatures.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables: CREE-ture. The plural is creatures. The verb create is a different word.
📖 Oxford: creature
13wildlife/ˈwaɪldlaɪf/noun
Definition
1. animals, birds, insects, etc. that are wild and live in a natural environment
★ Collocations: abundant wildlife; endangered wildlife; rare wildlife
★ Word family: (see OALD for derivatives)
  • The park protects endangered wildlife.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne word, no hyphen. Often paired with conservation.
📖 Oxford: wildlife
14fauna/ˈfɔːnə/noun
Definition
1. all the animals living in an area or in a particular period of history
★ Collocations: flora and fauna
★ Word family: (see OALD for derivatives)
  • The fauna of the rainforest includes monkeys and jaguars.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables: FAU-na. Don't confuse with flora (plants).
📖 Oxford: fauna
15flora/ˈflɔːrə/noun
Definition
1. the plants of a particular area, type of environment or period of time
★ Collocations: flora and fauna
★ Word family: (see OALD for derivatives)
  • The flora of Australia is unique.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables: FLOR-a. Don't confuse with fauna (animals).
📖 Oxford: flora
16species/ˈspiːʃiːz/noun
Definition
1. a group into which animals, plants, etc. that are able to have sex with each other and produce healthy young are divided, smaller than a genus
★ Collocations: living species; extinct species; common species
★ Word family: (see OALD for derivatives)
  • Many species are at risk of extinction.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallTwo syllables. Same form for singular and plural: “one species, two species”.
📖 Oxford: species
17flock/flɒk/noun
Definition
1. a group of sheep, goats
2. a large group of people, especially of the same type
3. the group of people who regularly attend the church of a particular priest, etc.
★ Collocations: flock (of something); flock (of somebody)
★ Word family: (see OALD for derivatives)
  • A flock of birds flew overhead.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne syllable. The verb flock to means to gather: “tourists flocked to the beach”.
📖 Oxford: flock
18herd/hɜːd/noun
Definition
1. a group of animals of the same type that live and feed together
2. a large group of people of the same type
3. to keep watch or control over somebody/something
★ Collocations: great herd; huge herd; large herd
★ Word family: (see OALD for derivatives)
  • A herd of elephants crossed the plain.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne syllable. Often used with herd mentality (following the crowd).
📖 Oxford: herd
19swarm/swɔːm/noun
Definition
1. a large group of insects, especially bees, moving together in the same direction
2. a large group of people, especially when they are all moving quickly in the same direction
★ Collocations: swarm (of something); swarm of bees/locusts/flies
★ Word family: (see OALD for derivatives)
  • A swarm of bees attacked the hive.
⚠ Native-speaker pitfallOne syllable. The verb swarm means to move in large numbers.
📖 Oxford: swarm
20throng/θrɒŋ/noun
Definition
1. a crowd of people

How this tool works

  • Select any word on the page (click + drag) — a small dictionary card pops up next to your selection with IPA, part of speech, a one-line definition, and a 🔊 button. If the word is in the glossary, you'll also see a link to jump to its full card.
  • Click any 🔊 button next to a word head to hear it pronounced aloud. Powered by the browser's built-in Web Speech API (no internet required once loaded). The voice uses your system's English voice — the best ones are usually Google US English, Microsoft Aria Online, or Microsoft Hazel.
  • Drag-select a phrase (e.g. tropical rainforest) — if all words in the phrase are vocabulary terms, the popup shows the closest match.
  • Type in the search bar to filter every card on the page by any word, example sentence, or part of speech. Matched text is highlighted.
  • Dark mode ☾ in the top-right for late-night study sessions — designed to keep your eyes fresh over long reading.

Authoritative sources

Every definition, IPA transcription, and example on this page is sourced from the Oxford Learner's Dictionary (OALD). Each word card ends with a direct link to its official entry, so you can always verify the exact meaning, register, and example sentences used by native-speaking lexicographers.
